title: Return, O Faithless Children
summary: Using the law of divorce, God asks whether an unfaithful wife could ever come back, and describes Judah's unfaithfulness in stark terms. He compares Judah with her sister Israel, the northern kingdom already sent into exile, and declares that Judah's pretended reform is worse. Then, astonishingly, he calls faithless Israel to return, promises shepherds after his own heart, a Jerusalem where the nations gather, and a reunited people, and the chapter ends with the words of repentance he longs to hear.
story: Chapter 2 laid out God's case against his people as an unfaithful bride. Chapter 3 carries the marriage image to its hardest question: after such betrayal, can the relationship be restored at all? The answer is shaped by history. The northern kingdom of Israel had been conquered by Assyria about a century earlier, and its people scattered. Judah watched and learned nothing. Yet the chapter's key word is return, repeated again and again, and it opens a door that chapter 4 will describe more fully: if the people truly turn back, God will heal them. This is the first bright line of hope in the book, and it points forward to the book of comfort in chapters 30 to 33.
historical:
Verse 6 dates part of this material to the days of King Josiah (about 640 to 609 BC). Josiah's reform, which gathered strength after 622 BC, removed pagan shrines in Judah and extended into the territory of the old northern kingdom, where he destroyed the altar at Bethel (2 Kings 23:15-20). The northern kingdom, Israel, had fallen to Assyria when Samaria was captured in 722 BC, and many of its people were deported. Jeremiah's call to proclaim toward the north (verse 12) addresses those scattered northerners, perhaps encouraged by Josiah's moves to reclaim the north.

The chapter also judges Josiah's reform. Judah returned only in pretense (verse 10): the outward changes did not reach the heart, and after Josiah's death the old practices came back quickly under his sons. Verse 16 speaks of the ark of the covenant being forgotten and not remade. The ark disappears from the biblical record at the fall of Jerusalem; the Bible does not say what became of it, though later Jewish legend, recorded in 2 Maccabees 2, claimed that Jeremiah hid it.
cultural:
Verse 1 alludes to the law of Deuteronomy 24:1-4. A man who divorced his wife with a written certificate could not remarry her after she had married another man and been divorced or widowed again; that would defile the land. Everyone knew the rule. God uses it to show how unthinkable restoration should be, and then he offers it anyway. The certificate of divorce in verse 8 comes from the same law.

The spring rains of verse 3 (the malqosh, the late rain of March and April) were essential for the grain to ripen before the dry summer. Baal worship claimed that the storm god controlled the rain; Jeremiah says the withholding of rain is the LORD's judgment on that very worship. Verse 2 compares Judah to a desert nomad, an Arab in Hebrew, waiting by the road to raid or to trade. In verse 24 the shameful god translates a Hebrew word, boshet (shame), that biblical writers sometimes substituted for Baal's name, as when Saul's son Eshbaal (1 Chronicles 8:33) is called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel.
literary: The chapter mixes poetry (verses 1 to 5 and 19 to 25) with a prose section (verses 6 to 18) dated to Josiah's reign. The Hebrew root shuv, to turn or return, runs through it with deliberate wordplay: the people are meshuvah (faithless, literally turning away) and are called to shuv (return), and God promises to heal their meshuvah (verse 22). The comparison of two sisters, Israel and Judah, anticipates Ezekiel's longer allegories in Ezekiel 16 and 23. The chapter ends in an unusual way: after God's invitation in verse 22, the people answer with a prayer of confession (verses 22 to 25), words that model the repentance God asks for, though chapter 4 will show that repentance must be real, not only spoken.

outline.t: Two unfaithful sisters: Israel and Judah
Shepherds, a new Jerusalem, a reunited people
Weeping on the heights: a prayer of repentance

doctrines.note: The chapter calls again and again for return. It also distinguishes true repentance from pretense: Judah returned outwardly under Josiah, but not with all her heart. Real repentance acknowledges guilt, turns from other gods, and comes to God as the only source of salvation.

The marriage covenant between God and his people has been broken, and by the law's own standard it could not be restored. God's offer to take his people back goes beyond what the law allows, rooted in his mercy rather than in their merit.

The future includes shepherds after God's own heart, a Jerusalem called the Throne of the LORD where the nations gather, and the reunion of Israel and Judah. Hope is grounded in God's promise to heal what the people cannot heal themselves.

words.note: Shuv, to turn or return, the key verb of repentance in the Old Testament. It means a change of direction: turning away from other gods and back to the LORD. Jeremiah uses the root more than almost any other book, and in this chapter it plays on itself, since the people's faithlessness (meshuvah) comes from the same root. Those who have turned away are called to turn back.

Meshuvah, faithlessness or backsliding, literally a turning away. Faithless Israel is almost a name in this chapter. God's promise in verse 22, I will heal your faithlessness, treats unfaithfulness as a sickness God himself will cure, not only a crime he will punish.

Bagad, to act treacherously or betray, used especially for breaking faith in a relationship, including marriage (Malachi 2:14-16). Verse 20 applies it to Israel: as a woman may betray her husband, so the people have betrayed God. The word keeps the issue personal; idolatry is not a religious mistake but a betrayal of love.

christ: The promise of shepherds after God's own heart (verse 15) recalls David, the man after God's own heart (1 Samuel 13:14), and anticipates Jeremiah 23:4-6, where God promises shepherds and a righteous branch from David's line. Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The vision of nations gathering in Jerusalem to honor the LORD's name, no longer following the stubbornness of their hearts, looks forward to the gospel reaching the nations, and the promise that the ark will not be missed suggests a future in which God's presence is no longer bound to a box in a temple; the New Testament locates that presence in Christ and in his people by the Spirit. The father who longs for his children to call him Father and return (verses 19 and 22) is echoed in Jesus's parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32), though the parable is not a quotation of this chapter.

hard.q: Why does God use such graphic sexual language for his people, and does it cast women in a bad light?
hard.a:
The chapter, like Hosea 1-3 and Ezekiel 16 and 23, pictures Israel as an unfaithful wife and uses blunt language of prostitution and adultery. Readers today rightly notice how uncomfortable this is, and some feminist interpreters argue that the image reinforces harmful views of women and of violence in marriage. Others respond that the metaphor's target is the whole nation, men and especially the male leaders (kings, priests, prophets), and that the prophets chose the most shocking image they had to expose idolatry as betrayal of love rather than a neutral religious choice.

It also helps to see how the chapter turns. By the law of Deuteronomy 24, a husband could not take back a wife who had married another. God, the wronged party in the metaphor, does exactly what the law would not require and begs his people to return. The image is harsh, but its point is the scandal of God's mercy. Readers should hold both: the metaphor is a product of its ancient setting and needs care, and its message is about God's grief and faithfulness, not about women.

questions: Judah returned in pretense but not with her whole heart. What are the signs of outward religious change that has not touched the heart?
God says, I will heal your faithlessness. How does it change your view of your own failures to think of them as something God wants to heal, not only to judge?
The chapter ends with a prayer of confession. What would it look like for you or your community to pray verses 22 to 25 honestly?
